paper_metadata.title: Revealing the Underlying Mechanism of Mechanical Properties Regulation in a Dual-Phase FeCrNi Medium Entropy Alloy via Thermomechanical Treatment
paper_metadata.journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

evidence.quote: This study investigates the evolution of microstructure and mechanical properties in a cold-rolled dual-phase Fe40Cr40Ni20 medium entropy alloy consisting of face-centered cubic (FCC) and body-centered cubic (BCC) phases, following annealing at different temperatures.

Five alloy ingots were prepared by arc-melting in an argon atmosphere, with a nominal composition of Fe 40Cr40Ni20 (at.%). The raw metals used had a purity of 99.99 wt%. To ensure homogeneity, each ingot was re-melted five times.
Solution treatment was conducted at 1200 C for 24 h, followed by water-quenching (WQ).
Alloy sheets with a thickness of 6 mm were cut from the remaining ingots and cold-rolled to a thickness of 1.8 mm, resulting in a 70% reduction.

evidence.quote: GNDs were mainly distributed in R1 and non-recrystallized grain in R2. As the annealing temperature increased, the density of GNDs gradually decreased.
In the cold-rolled state, the alloy demonstrates maximum strength but minimal ductility.
However, at an annealing temperature of 900 C, the fracture elongation sharply increased to 21.5%.

The strength of the alloy decreases with increasing annealing temperature, primarily influenced by the volume fractions of FCC and BCC phases, residual dislocation strengthening post-annealing, grain refinement, and back stress arising from the heterogeneous structure.
